Question: Ador or Amix?

↳ Posted by Kenny on November 29th, 2005.

Neither?

How about A-ind ( A indeterminate)? :-) Without a third in the scale, we can’t fairly accuse it of being either dorian or mixo. I wonder if there really is a name for it.

↳ Posted by Bob himself on December 1st, 2005.

“Bó Mhín Na Toitean Highland Fling” ~ A Dorian

There are problems with this transcription, but it is well gnawed away at bare bones. As a highland fling the parts would not repeat, the grand total being 16 bars. This also clarifies itself in the repetitive nature of the melody. Also, with regards to the discussion about key, it is played other ways and notes are picked up in the variations, including ‘C’. For example, taking just one bar, #4 of Part-B, here’s another simple take on it:

| d>ge>d (3cBA B>G | ~ I think that might settle it, as this would be C natural…

Indeterminate? ~ ;-) I like that…

↳ Posted by ceolachan on December 10th, 2005.

Bo Mhin na Toitean

Min na Toitean is atownland in N.W. Donegal. Johnny Doherty gave this tune which is a great variation of The Highland Lassie going to the Fair, the title of the cow and an equally good take on the Drunken Piper he titled the March of the Min na Toitean Bull. He probably heard them from older piping relatives and put his own unique stamp ,and names on them..

Does anyone know what the name translates to in English, I have nothing against Gaelic names but Bo Mhin Na Toitean is quite a mouthful

↳ Posted by Nopstavon on August 23rd, 2007.

“Bó Mhín Na Toitean” = “Barbecued Beef” :-/

The Mhín Na Toitean Cow

Bó = cow

Mhín Na Toitean = a geographic placename, County Donegal

toitean = toit = smoke

& with tóiteán = dóiteán = fire, conflagration, if you were desperate for something else you could always call it “Barbecued Beef”…

↳ Posted by Dr. Dow on August 27th, 2007.

Bagpipe strathspey / tuning

i adore the fierceness of this tune, as with many other strathspeys. since there is no natural “C” (D flat) that can be capacitated on the bagpipe scale, only “C sharp” (D) , and indeed this is very much a bagpipe tune of origin, then i must agree with the more “indeteminate” label for the tune, given the drones being in “A” (B flat). if the C sharp of the scale were given, i would say most definitely Mixolydian. the pentatonic nature of the tune gives an indication of its antiquity. i know that there are other versions written out that have a “C” in them, but in its purest form it is pentatonic, very obviously omitting any C or C sharp.

↳ Posted by Alistair Cassidy on July 23rd, 2011.

“what does ”mhin’ mean - in the context of the sentence that is ?"

Usually, meen, mine, min, mín or aspirated mhín in place names means a ‘smooth’ place - such as a smooth area on a hill, or a meadow. As for ‘toitean’: In Scots Gàidhlig it can mean more than just smoke or vapour - it could mean a piece of flesh, a steak or chop, a rick of corn, moles (on the skin) or a ‘small heap’ etc. Most likely it can be used similarly in Irish. A trip to Meenatotten might help you to work out its meaning.

↳ Posted by vonnieestes on July 8th, 2013.

The Drunken Piper

The tune played by Natalie McMaster is NOT the Drunken Piper. Can’t remember the name just now but something about a maid going to the fair. It is Hebridean and sounds like a wedding march (in Mairi’s Wedding style). The Drunken piper is a pipe march and is the chosen tune for “The Reel of the 51st Highland Division”, originally “The St Valery Reel”, composed by a group of officers from the 51st while in captivity during the Second World War. The dance was published in “The Victory Book” (otherwise Book 13) by the Royal Scottish Country Dance Society. For as writ performance pick out Jimmy Shand and Nicol Maclaren from the 25 recordings (there are many more) and pipe band performances on Youtube. None of the MIDI examples available above is correct, and some are just not the right tune.

↳ Posted by An Draighean on December 12th, 2016.

Re: Bó Mhín Na Toitean

I don’t know why this tune still gets associated with the Drunken Piper, Highland Rory, Far Am Bi Mi Fhin (?) or anything associated with the ‘meenatotten’ / Mhín Na Toitean bull (1950s?) - these all seem to me the same tune, (unless I’m wrong) published as Highland Rory ‘traditional’, by Willie Ross in 1869.

This tune is basically A Highland Lassie Going to the Fair, which is quite different to my ears, also published as ‘traditional’ and as a separate tune in the same publication.

Re: Bó Mhín Na Toitean

The tune, under the name “The Highland Lassie Going to the Fair”, is in the 19th century David Glen and William Ross collections. It is also in the Royal Scottish Piper’s collection. The dots can be found in the online Ceol Sean collection of collections. To my ear, quite old. Great fun to play on the border pipes.

Re: Bó Mhín Na Toitean

Some years ago I heard a story, I think it was from Caoimhin MacAoidh at Irish Fest in Milwaukee, about how this tune got its name “Bó Mhín Na Toitean” the gist of it was that Doherty senior (John’s father) and his sons were walking through a field when they realized there was a bull about to charge them. Doherty senior took out his fiddle and began to play a tune - this one I presume - and calmed the bull but the bull continued to follow them into town. They get inside safely slammed the door shut and asked for a whiskey, and then another. The landlord asked what the matter was and they told him of the bull. When the landlord asked “Where is the bull now?” Doherty replied at the door. The landlord opened the door saw the bull and slammed the door shut and told Doherty something like “I’ll give you a whole bottle if you lead him back to where he came from!”

You can hear the story in full, pretty much as I heard from Caoimhin and far better than I can tell it, on Vincent Campbell’s CD “Purple Heather” - (track 33 on disc 2). The title of the version which Vincent plays with the story on the next track is given as “The Drunken Piper”. I am guessing this is the tune that was played to calm the bull. This seems to be pretty much the same as the tune John Doherty gave as “The March of the MeenaToiten Bull” on Bundle & Go.
